chapter: Suntaug Lake Inn and Duke Ellington's band
title: The 1939-40 Duke band
summary: They agree it was the greatest band, naming Ray Nance, Tricky Sam, Hamilton, Rex Stewart and Ben, and Whaley praises their interpretation.

story.theme_name: Duke Ellington and his orchestra, as others knew them
story.community_name: Duke Ellington: the band, the man, his men

blocks.x: If you were there, you were copying for them, those were probably the greatest years of Duke's band, would you say. Most people have said that 1940 band --
That 1939 and '40 band was the greatest band, right.
Now, who were those guys. Ray Nance came in about that time.
Yeah, Ray Nance come in.
Tricky Sam was still there, right.
Right.
Who else, name some other guys.
Whetzel --
No, Whetzel was gone in 1940.
Johnny -- Jimmy Hamilton.
Rex Stewart was there.
Yeah, Rex Stewart, that's it.
And Ben was there. In 1940
Yeah. That was a great band.
That was one of the great bands and
the critics and most people in show business have always admitted that.

Yeah, to me that was a great band, see. Because the guys understood, you know, and they would play and bend a note, they could bend a note instead of playing it just as a quarter note or half note or eighth note, they would bend it and play it this way. Give it some color and everything. Interpretation of his music was great.
No question about that.
And what are some of the tunes that you think were some of his greatest masterpieces you copied for him.
Let me see, 'Black, Brown & Beige' I think was the greatest. That developed all that stuff in there.
Did that develop in My People.

Yeah, that came in with My People, but Ray Nance was in there on the violin. He had a part on his violin and man, he was great. Soul, really a soul man. He would play that violin and get on to one of them notes.
Ray and I went to high school together in Chicago.
In Chicago, yeah.
It was a great loss.
He was a great guy.
